title: How Faraday Cages Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Faraday cages: conductive enclosures that keep electric charge and electromagnetic radiation out (and sometimes in). They cover Ben Franklin's 1755 pint-can and cork-ball observations, Michael Faraday's room and ice pail experiments, the physics of electrostatic induction, and applications including microwave doors, MRI rooms, labs, airplanes and cars struck by lightning, shielded government rooms, and EMF-allergy and survivalist claims. They also discuss a Dutch computer expert's electromagnetic eavesdropping on voting machines. The episode ends with a listener email suggesting an electric eel episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and drinks
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about drinks (Topo Chico, tequila), a lightning-strike question, and the Faraday name, setting up the topic.

segments.title: What a Faraday cage is and Ben Franklin's observations
segments.summary: A Faraday cage is a conductor surrounding something to protect it from electric charge or electromagnetic radiation. Ben Franklin in 1755 lowered an uncharged cork ball into an electrified pint can and saw it did not pick up charge; Michael Faraday later investigated the effect decades on.

segments.title: Faraday's experiments and the ice pail
segments.summary: Faraday recreated the experiments, including sitting inside a foil-lined room with charge applied outside, and used an ice pail (a bucket, now made of wire mesh) to show the charge stays on the exterior.

segments.title: Electrostatic induction explained
segments.summary: Using a pint can as an example, the hosts explain how a charged object pulls opposite charges to the near side of a conductor and pushes like charges away, so the charge stays on the outside and the inside is neutral.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break; no sponsor read is present in the transcript.

segments.title: Shielding strength and real-world applications
segments.summary: Shielding depends on the metal, conductivity, and mesh hole size relative to wavelength; plaster and lath walls and rebar can act as partial cages. Applications include university labs, MRI rooms, and airplanes, which are Faraday cages and are sometimes struck by lightning.

segments.title: EMF allergies, secure rooms, and eavesdropping
segments.summary: The hosts discuss EMF allergy claims as largely unsupported by science, government secure rooms that block leakage, and Rop Gonggrijp's demonstration of electromagnetic eavesdropping on Dutch voting machines.

segments.title: Survivalists and EMP protection
segments.summary: Preppers build Faraday cages to protect electronics from electromagnetic pulses, though a cage is useless if you are outside it during an event. Shielding wallpaper and mu-metal are mentioned as options.

segments.title: Off-topic chat about sleep and email
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss their sleep habits and scheduling emails.

segments.title: Listener email suggesting electric eels
segments.summary: A listener from Poland suggests an episode on electric eels, noting how little is known about them, and the hosts respond warmly.
